title: Reading Drawings
short_answer: Every sheet has a letter and number — find the title block, grid lines, and written dimensions. Never scale off the drawing; a conflict between documents is an RFI, not a field decision.
summary: A drawing set is an organized system. Learn the organization once and you can find anything in any set, on any job, for the rest of your career.
plain_words: Every sheet has a letter and a number. The letter says whose drawing it is — A is the architect's, S is structural, M P E are mechanical, plumbing, and electrical. Find the title block for the sheet name, scale, and revision. Find the grid lines — that's what everything gets measured from. Use the written dimension. Never hold a ruler up to a drawing.
when_to_use: Day one on any job — before layout, framing, or hang
When you need a partition type, finish level, rated wall, or opening size
Before building anything where two sheets might disagree
prerequisites: Current drawing set with revision noted in the title block
Access to partition schedule, life safety plan, and finish schedule for the job

tools.name: Highlighter or pencil for wall tags and clouds

steps.title: Title block
steps.body: Bottom right or down the right edge — sheet name, number, scale, date, revision, and seal. Read the revision first.

steps.title: Scale
steps.body: 1/4" = 1'-0" is the usual floor plan; 1/8" on big buildings; 1-1/2" or 3" on details. A detail is drawn large because the small stuff matters there — still use written dimensions.

steps.title: North arrow
steps.body: Orients you so "the east corridor" stops being a guess.

steps.title: Grid lines and bubbles
steps.body: Lettered one way, numbered the other, circles at the ends — the building's coordinate system. Layout comes from here.

steps.title: Dimension strings
steps.body: Chains locating walls. Note whether they run to face of stud, face of finish, or centerline — stated on the plan; getting it wrong shifts every wall.

steps.title: Section and detail callouts
steps.body: Circle or flag with two numbers: top = detail number, bottom = sheet it's drawn on. Chase details across the set.

steps.title: Keynotes and tags
steps.body: Small numbers or letters on the plan, decoded in a legend on the same sheet or in the general sheets.

steps.title: Clouds and delta symbols
steps.body: Cloud around an area with a numbered triangle means that part changed — read what changed before you build it.

steps.title: Wall tag on plan
steps.body: Find the tag at the wall — e.g. A3.

steps.title: Partition schedule
steps.body: Look up the tag — stud depth, gauge, spacing, board type and layers, fire rating, wall height.

steps.title: To ceiling or to deck
steps.body: Note which — it changes the whole top of the wall.

steps.title: Rated assembly
steps.body: If rated, find the listed assembly number and the head-of-wall detail that goes with it.

steps.title: Finish schedule
steps.body: Cross-check the room for finish level and sheen you are building toward.

steps.title: Door schedule
steps.body: Cross-check any opening in that wall for rough opening and frame type.

warnings.title: Never scale off a drawing
warnings.body: Sets get printed, reduced, emailed, and photographed. A sheet that says 1/4" scale may not be at 1/4" anymore. If there is no written dimension for what you need, that is a question — not a measurement.

warnings.title: Check the revision before you build
warnings.body: Building accurately off a superseded sheet is still building it wrong — the most expensive mistake on this page.

warnings.title: Partition schedule is home base
warnings.body: G (general) sheets hold the legend. A sheets are architectural — floor plans, partition types, RCP, elevations, details. S = structural deflection and bracing. M/P/E = what goes in our walls and above our ceilings. The partition schedule turns every wall tag into stud, board, rating, and height.

experts.summary: Change orders and addenda beat original drawings. Later revision beats earlier. Approved submittals govern the product installed. Manufacturer instructions govern installation. Spec vs drawings is project-specific — read that project's precedence clause; do not assume. A conflict between contract documents is an RFI, not a field decision — write the question and work elsewhere while you wait. A good RFI names both sheets, states what each requires, proposes an answer, and says what is held up.

Residential: smaller sets, wall types often on the plan or assumed, dimensions commonly to face of framing, limited rated walls, questions often by phone, changes often verbal — which is why GVC change-order documentation matters more on residential, not less. Commercial: formal partition schedule on every wall, dimensions often to face of finish or grid, extensive rated walls with life safety plan, formal RFIs, priced change orders. The trap: a commercial hand assuming missing info means "do whatever's normal," or a residential hand not opening a schedule that governs the wall.

variations.title: Discipline letters (NCS convention)
changes: M / P / E = mechanical, plumbing, electrical rough-in
FP or F = fire protection through our ceilings
C / L = civil, landscape — rarely ours

variations.title: Sheets we live on
changes: Partition / wall type schedule — stud, board, rating, height
Floor plans — wall locations and dimensions
Reflected ceiling plan — read like floor plan, not flipped
Life safety plan — rated walls at a glance
Finish schedule — finish level and sheen we owe
Door and frame schedule — rough openings
Details — head of wall, control joints, transitions

quality_checks.prompt: Title block revision checked before layout or build
Located dimensions from written strings — never scaled with a ruler
Partition schedule opened for every wall tag before framing or board
Document conflicts written as RFI — not built as a field guess

common_mistakes.title: Building off a superseded revision
common_mistakes.wrong: Use the sheet that was on the table without checking revision
common_mistakes.right: Read revision block first; chase clouds on revised sheets
common_mistakes.why: Accurate work on the wrong revision still gets demolished

common_mistakes.title: Scaling with a ruler
common_mistakes.wrong: Measure off the printed sheet when no dimension is shown
common_mistakes.right: Ask for a dimension or write an RFI
common_mistakes.why: Reduced or photographed sets are not true scale

common_mistakes.title: Never opening the partition schedule
common_mistakes.wrong: Build every wall the same way
common_mistakes.right: Look up every wall tag before studs go up
common_mistakes.why: Rating, board layers, and height all live on the schedule

common_mistakes.title: Wrong dimensioning convention
common_mistakes.wrong: Assume face of stud when the plan dimensions to face of finish
common_mistakes.right: Read the plan note on dimensioning basis
common_mistakes.why: Shifts every wall in the run

common_mistakes.title: Choosing between conflicting documents
common_mistakes.wrong: Pick the detail that looks right and build
common_mistakes.right: RFI with both sources named; work elsewhere while waiting
common_mistakes.why: Guess becomes our rework at our cost

common_mistakes.title: Missing clouded revisions
common_mistakes.wrong: Ignore revision clouds on a reissued sheet
common_mistakes.right: Read every cloud and delta before mobilizing that area
common_mistakes.why: Changes hide in the clouded zones

common_mistakes.title: Skipping finish schedule
common_mistakes.wrong: Assume Level 4 until the painter arrives
common_mistakes.right: Cross-check room finish level before finishing mobilizes
common_mistakes.why: Level 5 or skim scope missed at bid hurts margin

common_mistakes.title: Skipping life safety plan
common_mistakes.wrong: Hunt rated walls only from memory
common_mistakes.right: Use life safety plan to find rated walls fast
common_mistakes.why: Unrated assembly on a rated line fails inspection

provenance.note: Sheet numbering follows the widely used National CAD Standard convention — most commercial sets in our market use it, though not all; read the set's own index. Scales, title block, grids, and callouts are standard drafting practice. Document precedence is project-specific — read each project's clause. Residential/commercial comparison reflects GVC's mix of work.
